method: Authored Phase-2-first: for each of the 29 policy concepts, the Phase 1 codebook themes whose definition it plausibly answers. Interpretive, not measured — no edge implies any respondent endorsed the concept, only that their raised theme is thematically continuous with it. A theme cited by no concept is not listed here; it is derived as 'unclaimed' at build time, not hand-picked.

sources.rationale: "Protect workers" is the direct government-action ask this concept enacts.
"Job losses and displacement" is the economic worry this concept responds to.
"Own job feels at risk" is the personal experience behind wanting jobs kept/added.
A stronger, ban-shaped cousin of the same demand — incentivizing retention overlaps with banning replacement.
"Retraining and transition funding" is exactly what shifting/reskilling employees asks government to fund.
"Leaving the field" is the lived version of needing to shift roles.
"Pressure to learn AI skills" motivates a reskilling policy response.
"Searching in a flooded market" is adjacent to needing a path to a new role.
Universal basic income is a direct form of support for displaced workers.
"Share the gains" is the broader redistribution rationale for supporting job-losers.
"Already lost work" is the lived experience this concept is a policy response to.
"The jobs left are worse jobs" is the condition support policies are meant to offset.
"Make AI replacement of workers illegal" is the closest direct government-action match, even though this concept is framed narrowly around firing-for-non-adoption.
"Required to use it" is the personal experience of being pressured to adopt AI or else.
General worker protection covers this narrower prohibition.
"It showed up in the software" — imposed tooling is adjacent to imposed use.
"Conditions on AI-driven layoffs" includes reporting requirements like this concept.
"Corporate disclosure" is the general transparency principle behind reporting job loss.
The economic concern this reporting requirement would track.
"A tool, not a replacement" is exactly the framing of using AI for undesirable/impossible tasks rather than replacing workers.
"Efficiency and growth" is the economic upside this framing leans on.
"Found it useful" is the personal-level analog of AI doing unwanted work well.
"Corporate disclosure" is the direct ask behind using data properly and transparently.
"Privacy and surveillance limits" covers proper data use.
"Consent and payment for training data" is a specific instance of proper data use.
"Own work used without consent" is the personal harm improper data use causes.
Direct match: privacy limits are what preserving privacy asks for.
"Monitored by AI at work" is the personal experience privacy protection responds to.
Limiting data collection is a specific mechanism of privacy/surveillance limits.
Disclosure of what's collected is adjacent to limiting collection.
"Screened by AI while job-hunting" is a lived instance of data being collected and used on a person.
Direct match: "Let people turn it off."
"Chooses not to use it" is the lived version of wanting an opt-out.
Being met by AI as a customer is the context in which opting out matters.
Direct match: "Label AI-generated output."
Disclosure of AI use generally is the broader principle this concept enacts.
"Was given wrong information" is a harm labelling/disclosure is meant to prevent.
Direct match: "A human has to decide."
"Loss of the human element" is the personal experience this concept guards against.
General oversight is adjacent to requiring human sign-off.
Access to a life outside AI is the broader version of the opt-out ask.
"Colleagues losing the ability" is the concern over-reliance on AI raises, which this concept addresses by preserving non-AI life.
"How work is valued" touches the same concern about AI crowding out human experience.
Distinguishing AI from human output is a conceptual precursor to labelling it.
Confusion about what's AI-generated is a source of being misinformed.
Defining the AI/human boundary relates to preserving the human element.
Direct match: "Schools and education policy."
"Harm to students' learning" is the concern improved AI education addresses.
Pressure to learn AI skills extends to students as future workers.
"Teaching and assessment upended" is exactly the classroom problem this concept responds to.
General education policy covers rules on student AI use.
Harm to learning is the rationale for restricting AI use on schoolwork.
Parental controls for AI use fall under education/child-safety policy.
General safety oversight extends to protecting minors.
"Protect people the systems interact with" covers protecting children specifically.
Direct match: "Let the affected public decide."
"Legislate with people who understand it" is a complementary form of broadened input.
Fear that "industry will control the process" is the reason public input is demanded.
Distrust that government alone will get it right also motivates wanting public input.
The community-scoped version of the same public-input demand as C-18.
Communities near data centers are a concrete case of needing input on local AI impacts.
"Local environmental cost" is a typical AI-related impact communities would want input on.
Direct match: "Names acceptable uses."
Determining safe fields of use is a form of safety oversight.
Naming where AI is safe implies restricting it elsewhere.
Restricting AI in hiring is one instance of a field where use is deemed unsafe.
Direct, broad match: "Regulate, unspecified."
Controlling how AI works is a core safety-oversight function.
Criminalizing specific misuses is one mechanism of controlling AI behavior.
"Doubts the work is any good" is a concern that controlling how AI works would address.
"Consent and payment for training data" is the core copyright mechanism.
Direct match on the copyright topic, from the opposite (AI-output) side.
"Protect creative professions" is the constituency copyright enforcement serves.
"Own work used without consent" is the personal harm this concept remedies.
Direct match: "Rules for government's own use of AI."
Efficiency gains are the stated rationale for using AI in government operations.
"Tax and financial levers" is a direct mechanism for restricting profits.
Restricting profits is a form of limiting/curbing company behavior.
"How the gains get captured" is the economic concern behind restricting profits.
Concern over unchecked corporate power motivates profit restriction.
Direct match: "Legal accountability for harms."
"Protect people the systems interact with" is exactly consumer accountability.
Criminal accountability is a stronger form of the same demand.
"The public doesn't want it" is the sentiment behind demanding accountability.
Direct match: "Control where facilities are built."
"Data centres pay their own way" is the core protect-consumers-from-resource-needs mechanism.
"Environmental and energy impact" is the general policy area this concept sits in.
"Local environmental cost" is the lived version of the same resource-needs concern.
"Energy and water bills" is the consumer-cost angle data-center resource use raises.
Public awareness campaigns fall under the general education-policy ask.
Awareness of ethical use would reduce being misled by AI outputs.
General AI literacy overlaps with feeling pressure to learn AI skills.
Direct match: "Pause and study first."
"Look to other jurisdictions or history" is a specific research strategy.
Not knowing what to expect is the uncertainty more research is meant to resolve.
Employer AI training is a specific instance of the broader retraining/transition-funding ask.
"Pressure to learn AI skills" is what employee training responds to.
"Deployed without preparation" is the failure mode training is meant to prevent.
